passage: Hans Hofmann's art is recognized increasingly as a major fountainhead of style and ideas for the "new" American painting, yet its value, independent of its influence and of Hofmann's role as a teacher, is still the object of qualifications. He is important but ignored. His omission from the "New American Painting" show that The Museum of Modern Art sent to Europe (1958 - 59) is a case in point (an omission which did more to question the show's taste than did the number of highly questionable inclusions). A good share of the blame rests with the public's attitude towards advanced art, which usually asks that a "difficult" artist confine himself to a single readily identifiable artistic approach before it will take trouble with him. The art world wants an artist to commit to one style. One would think that the exhilaration and satisfaction to be gotten from following advanced art were proportionate to the effort of discrimination required, but most of those who do the following do not seem to agree. Having accepted modern art, the public wants it to be made easy to understand, apparently. And so Hofmann himself is also to blame in some part. And actually, the more excellence I find in his art the more I am inclined to shift the blame toward him. The variety of manners and even of styles in which he works confuses the public. At the same time, such a diversity of manners makes one suspect an undue absorption in problems and challenges for their own sake. Or else this artist too implicitly follows wherever his inventive fertility leads him instead of bending that fertility to his vision. And Hofmann's inventiveness is truly enormous, to the point where he might be called a virtuoso of invention, such as only the Klee of the 1930s was before him. But, in art one cannot scatter one's shots with impunity, and Hofmann has paid a certain price, in terms of quality as well as acceptance, for doing so. The price is certainly not as large as the price Klee paid in the 1930s, but it may be larger than the one Klee paid in his prime (when his "hand-written" approach and the small formats to which he restricted himself conferred a real unity of style upon all the different notational systems he used). And unlike Picasso since 1917, Hofmann has no main style that governs all others; he can work in as many as three or four different ones in the span of a year and give them all equal emphasis. The notion of experiment has been much abused in connection with modernist art, but Hofmann's painting would seem to justify its introduction if anything does. Hofmann is perhaps the most difficult artist alive, difficult to grasp and to appreciate. But by the same token he is an immensely interesting, original, and rewarding one, whose troubles in clarifying his art stem in large part precisely from the fact that he has so much to say. And though he may belong to the same moment in the evolution of easel painting as Pollock, he is even less categorizable. He has been called a "German Expressionist," yet little in what is known as Expressionism, aside from Kandinsky's swirl, predicts him. His color and color textures may be "Nordic," but one clutches at this adjective in despair at a resolute originality in which the "Mediterranean" is assimilated.

questions.question: The passage implies that an artist is difficult to understand when he:
options: Option A: is inventive.
Option B: is modern.
Option C: avoids using a style.
Option D: uses different styles.

questions.question: The author of the passage would be most likely to agree with which of the following ideas expressed by other art critics.
options: Option A: Traditional art is easier to understand than modern art.
Option B: The great artists are the ones that transform art history.
Option C: Knowing the artist's life helps one to know the artwork.
Option D: How one paints is as important as what one opts to paint.
questions.correct: Option D: How one paints is as important as what one opts to paint

questions.question: The claim that Hans Hofman is a painter that does not receive the attention he deserves is based mainly on the:
options: Option A: the comparison between Hofman and Picasso.
Option B: decisions made by the Museum of Modern Art.
Option C: how Paul Klee's work was received by the art world.
Option D: importance of Hofman's contributions to modern art.
questions.correct: Option B: decisions made by the Museum of Modern Art.

questions.question: Regarding Picasso (paragraph 4), the passage strongly implies that:
options: Option A: he used multiple styles.
Option B: he was not accepted during his time.
Option C: he was a difficult artist.
Option D: he was a very interesting artist.
questions.correct: Option A: he used multiple styles.

questions.question: Passage information indicates that which of the following statements must be true?
options: Option A: Multi-style painters produce work that is different from painters with just one style
Option B: Painterly styles are as unique to painters as are fingerprints.
Option C: Art critics believe that one definition of a bad painter is one who lacks a style.
Option D: To paint as modern painters do, one should stick to one style.
questions.correct: Option A: Multi-style painters produce work that is different from painters with just one style

questions.question: Information in the first paragraph suggest that the author probably believes that public opinion:
options: Option A: rarely differs from the opinions of art critics.
Option B: has an effect on how an artist chooses to paint.
Option C: likes identifying an artist with a specific style.
Option D: accepts that modern art deserves to be displayed.
questions.correct: Option C: likes identifying an artist with a specific style.
